newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British fraudbusters win 5th BCCI conviction.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British fraudbusters win 5th BCCI conviction.

text.p: Abbas Gokal, head of the largest single borrower from the failed Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), on Thursday became the fifth person to be convicted for his part in the biggest known banking fraud.
Gokal was found guilty at London's Central Criminal Court of conspiring to account falsely and of conspiracy to defraud following a trial lasting nearly five months.
He is expected to be sentenced on May 6 and faces a maximum prison sentence of 17 years.
Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) said Gokal, 61, had with BCCI officials "masterminded a massive fraud totalling approximately $1.2 billion".
BCCI collapsed in 1991 with debts of more than $12 billion after evidence emerged of widespread money laundering. Thousands of people lost their savings.
English liquidators Deloitte & Touche are pursuing claims against various parties as a result of the bank's demise and Gokal's conviction will have implications for this, legal sources said.
There are civil cases pending against both Gokal and his Gulf shipping and trading group and further action is expected against him in Pakistan.
The liquidators are also pursuing substantial claims against the Bank of England and auditors Price Waterhouse and Ernst & Whinney, now part of the merged Ernst & Young.
So far creditors have received $2.65 billion, equal to 24.5 percent of their claims, and a further 10 percent is expected to be paid within the next year.
The SFO, which investigates and prosecutes major financial fraud in Britain, said the BCCI case was the biggest fraud in banking history and the largest ever fraud trial.
BCCI's symbiotic relationship with Gokal's Swiss-based Mideast Gulf group meant the fortunes of the two were inextricably linked.
So far, investigating and prosecuting those responsible has cost around 15 million pounds ($24.6 million), including the four million pound cost of Gokal's case.
Some estimates put the total cost of the Gokal trial, including the legal aid he received for his defence, at closer to 10 million pounds.

The SFO told Reuters it had applied for confiscation and compensation orders against Gokal. If successful, these would enable it to seize his assets, believed to total up to 20 million pounds, and pass them to the liquidators to repay creditors.
Chris Dickson, the SFO lawyer heading the BCCI inquiry team, said Gokal's actions had "brought despair to hundreds of thousands of ordinary people who put their savings into BCCI".

Dickson said these people were proof "that human misery is the real cost of fraud". One of the individual losers was Anant Shah, who lost the money he had saved for a bone marrow transplant for his son.
The biggest loser was the Western Isles Council in Scotland, which was owed 24 million pounds.
The SFO said it had found documents signed by Gokal in a London safe deposit box showing he and his two brothers owned and controlled the companies involved in the fraud.
The prosecution had said that the sums received from BCCI supported Gokal's lavish lifestyle. Gokal travelled by company jet and owned several luxury cars, including two Rolls-Royces.

It said Gokal had needed large sums of money for his ailing business empire when the recession started to bite during the 1980s. BCCI funded him with such large amounts that much of the lending had to be diguised because the bank was breaking guidelines.
Gokal, who denied the charges against him, fled from his company base in Geneva, Switzerland, to Pakistan in 1992 after Gulf collapsed.

He was arrested by German police at Frankfurt airport in July 1994 when the plane he was travelling on landed for refuelling on a flight from Karachi to the United States. He was extradited to Britain and has been in custody since his arrival in December 1994.
His conviction is a boost to the SFO, which has received far more attention for its failures than its successes in prosecuting lengthy cases.
It has an overall conviction rate of around 63 percent and has had considerable success with its BCCI cases.

"This is a good result for those who say that juries can cope with long trials," said one legal source. There have been calls for scrapping jury trials in fraud cases by those who argue lay jurors cannot get to grips with complex financial cases.
